query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, removing Co shifts the local dislocation behavior such that under dynamic loading the alloy preferentially forms an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or partially amorphous) layer at internal boundaries. This transient, deformation‐induced substructure enhances strain hardening and ductility at high strain rates, while at lower strain rates and temperatures the absence of Co yields a different balance of dislocation slip and recovery compared to the equiatomic alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase solid solution with equiaxed grains similar to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline, but lacking Co.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled tensile (or compressive) tests over a matrix of strain rates (from quasi‐static ~10^–3 s^–1 to dynamic ~10^0–10^3 s^–1) and temperatures (e.g., room temperature up to an elevated temperature below recrystallization) to induce dynamic deformation.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in the single‐phase, non‐precipitated (solid-solution) regime, where the temperature is below the recrystallization point and strain rates are varied to activate dislocation dynamics and associated local deformation processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or partially amorphous layer at grain boundaries and other internal interfaces arising during dynamic deformation.
generation.mechanism: Dynamic deformation initiates enhanced dislocation activity whose local interactions in the absence of Co (which normally modifies the dislocation core and stacking fault energy) lead to a strain‐induced restructuring at grain boundaries. This dynamic amorphization (or nano‐refinement) mediates a favorable balance between strength and ductility by increasing strain hardening during high-rate loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co‐free alloy should exhibit a notable strain-rate and temperature dependent effect: at low strain rates, it may show slightly lower yield strength and a conventional ductility response, whereas at high strain rates the onset of dynamic formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer will boost strain hardening and maintain or improve ductility and strength relative to the equiatomic alloy.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, which under similar loading conditions does not form the same degree of dynamic substructure (i.e., less dynamic amorphization at high strain rates) and thus follows a more typical dislocation slip-dominated behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the solidified, single‐phase solid-solution state below any phase transformation/recrystallization temperature, and specifically in the deformation regime where dislocation-driven mechanisms (including dynamic nano‐refinement or amorphization) are active.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical strain rate and temperature thresholds at which the dynamic substructure forms are unknown, and the degree to which the absence of Co alters stacking fault energies or dislocation core structures remains to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline. Perform a series of tensile (or compression) tests at multiple strain rates (from quasi‐static to dynamic) and at selected temperatures below recrystallization. Use in situ electron microscopy (TEM or EBSD) to monitor the evolution of grain/subgrain structure and identify the presence of ultra‐nanocrystalline (or amorphous) layers at grain boundaries during deformation.
measurements: Strain rate sensitivity of flow stress
Grain size evolution and evidence of dynamic amorphization (via in situ TEM/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co‐free alloy does not exhibit a strain-rate and temperature dependent formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous substructure — or if its strength–ductility balance is not measurably different from that of the equiatomic alloy under identical testing conditions — then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
